title: The largest in every window

prereqs.why: Each index is pushed once and popped once, which is what makes the whole pass linear even though the inner loops look expensive.
A deque is the structure being used, and you have built one.
The invariant - the deque holds indices in decreasing order of value - is what makes the front the answer.

statement:
Read `n` and `k`, then `n` integers.

If `k` is less than 1 or greater than `n`, print

```
no windows
```

and stop. Otherwise print the number of windows on the first line, and on
the second the maximum of each window of `k` consecutive values, in order,
separated by single spaces.

### The sample

```
8 3
1 3 -1 -3 5 3 6 7
```

```
6
3 3 5 5 6 7
```

### What is being asked for

The obvious solution scans each window and costs `O(n*k)`. This one is
to be **one pass**, with each element looked at a bounded number of
times in total — `O(n)` overall.

The structure that does it is a double-ended queue of **indices**, kept
so that the values they point at are in decreasing order. Then the front
is always the maximum of the current window, and the two things to do on
each step are: drop the front if it has fallen out of the window, and
drop from the back anything the new element beats.

Values fit in a 64-bit signed integer.
hints: Store indices in the deque, not values. You need the index to know when an element has fallen out of the left-hand end of the window.
Two while-loops before you push, and the order matters: first drop the front if `q.front() <= i - k`, then drop from the back while the back's value is no greater than the new one.
Only start printing once a full window exists, which is from `i == k - 1` onwards. There are `n - k + 1` windows in all.

Why it is linear: each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the total work of the inner loops over the whole run is at most `n` pops. Individual steps can be slow; the average over the pass cannot.
